```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = TRUE
)
```

This article shows how to get environmental values inside 3D shapes, such as
tag detections, buffers around them, a tag's track, or a protected area down to
a set depth.
Each example uses the same three steps:

1. **Build** the shapes with `as_vector3d()` or `buffer_3d()`.
2. **Intersect** each shape with the data: `crop()` the dataset to the shape,
   read its time steps with `as_voxel()`, and keep the values inside the shape
   with `mask()`.
3. **Summarise** the values with `summarise_3d()`.

You loop over the shapes yourself, so you can stop after any step and look at
the result. Each example ends with a table of values per shape, which you can
join back to your observations. Volumes are in km³ throughout.

## Example data

The examples use a small synthetic temperature dataset: a 0.05° grid off
eastern Australia, six depth levels from 0 to 200 m, and five daily time
steps. Temperature falls with depth, rises to the north and warms a little
each day. The code below writes it to a netCDF file, as you might download
from Copernicus Marine.

```{r data}
library(ocean3d)

lon <- seq(150.025, 150.975, by = 0.05)
lat <- seq(-20.975, -20.025, by = 0.05)
depth <- c(0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200)
time <- 0:4
grid <- expand.grid(lon = lon, lat = lat, depth = depth, time = time)
temp <- 28 - 0.06 * grid$depth + 2 * (grid$lat + 20.5) + 0.2 * grid$time

dims <- list(
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("lon", "degrees_east", lon),
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("lat", "degrees_north", lat),
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("depth", "m", depth),
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("time", "days since 2020-03-01", time)
)
var <- ncdf4::ncvar_def("temp", "degC", dims, missval = -9999,
                        prec = "double")
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".nc")
nc <- ncdf4::nc_create(path, var)
ncdf4::ncvar_put(nc, var, array(temp, lengths(lapply(dims, `[[`, "vals"))))
ncdf4::nc_close(nc)
```

`as_proxy()` describes the file without reading its values. Each later step
reads only the cells and time steps it needs, at every depth level.

```{r proxy}
proxy <- as_proxy(path)
proxy
```

## Points: tag detections

Three detections, each with a position, a depth and a date, become
`SpatVector3D` points:

```{r points}
obs <- data.frame(
  tag = c("A", "B", "C"),
  lon = c(150.21, 150.52, 150.80),
  lat = c(-20.31, -20.56, -20.82),
  depth = c(12, 48, 140),
  date = as.Date(c("2020-03-01", "2020-03-02", "2020-03-04"))
)
detections <- as_vector3d(obs, time = "date", id = "tag")
detections
```

For one detection, `crop()` keeps the grid cell it falls in, and `as_voxel()`
reads the time step nearest its date. With a shape as `time`, `as_voxel()`
always returns a list, here with one voxel. `mask()` then keeps the value at
the depth level nearest the detection's depth:

```{r one-point}
a <- detections[1]
v <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, a), time = a)[[1]]
summarise_3d(mask(v, a), statistic = "mean")
```

Detection A at 12 m takes the 10 m level. `extract_to_point()` gives the same
value from the file:

```{r extract-to-point}
extract_to_point(obs[1, ], path, var = "temp", date_col = "date",
                 method = "nearest")$temp
```

Both pick the nearest time step: on this data they give the same values for
all three detections, for a time halfway between two steps, and for a date
after the last step. `extract_to_point()` warns when the step it picks is on
another day; `as_voxel()` doesn't, so set `max_time_diff` in `as_voxel()` to
limit how far away the step may be.

The two differ when the nearest depth level has no value. `extract_to_point()`
skips depth levels with no value when it looks for the nearest one. `mask()`
uses the nearest level whatever its value, so such a detection gets `NA`.

## Buffers: the water around each detection

`buffer_3d()` turns each detection into a polygon: here a circle of 5 km
radius, from 20 m above to 20 m below the detection, and one day either side.

```{r buffers}
buffers <- buffer_3d(detections, radius_km = 5, depth_window = 20,
                     time_window = 1)
as.data.frame(buffers)[c("feature_id", "depth_min", "depth_max",
                         "time_start", "time_end")]
```

The steps are the same as for one detection, run for each buffer in turn.
`as_voxel()` returns one voxel for each time step inside a buffer's window:
three for B and C, and two for A, whose window starts before the first day of
data. Given that list of voxels, `summarise_3d()` gives one row per time
step. By default the mean is weighted by the volume of water each value
stands for, and `n` counts the values used.

`mask()` uses only a buffer's outline and depth range, because `as_voxel()`
has already used its time. It prints a message saying so each time, which
`suppressMessages()` hides inside the loop.

```{r buffer-loop}
buffer_rows <- lapply(seq_along(buffers), function(i) {
  b <- buffers[i]
  voxels <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, b), time = b)
  inside <- lapply(voxels, function(v) suppressMessages(mask(v, b)))
  rows <- summarise_3d(inside, statistic = c("mean", "sd"))
  cbind(feature_id = as.data.frame(b)$feature_id, rows)
})
do.call(rbind, buffer_rows)
```

Each row summarises one time step; `summarise_3d()` doesn't pool values
across steps.

## Tracks: buffers along a route

A track is a line with a depth and a time at each vertex. This tag records
three positions over a day and a quarter:

```{r track}
route <- data.frame(
  tag = "D",
  lon = c(150.15, 150.45, 150.85),
  lat = c(-20.85, -20.50, -20.40),
  depth = c(5, 60, 20),
  time = as.POSIXct(c("2020-03-02 00:00", "2020-03-02 12:00",
                      "2020-03-03 06:00"), tz = "UTC")
)
track <- as_vector3d(route, type = "lines", id = "tag", time = "time")
```

One buffer around the whole line would cover its whole depth and time range,
from 5 m to 60 m and over both days. To follow the route more closely,
`sample_3d()` places points along it, here at most 10 km apart. Each point
gets the depth and time interpolated between the vertices either side, and
`support_km`, the length of route it stands for: half the distance to the
points either side.

```{r samples}
samples <- sample_3d(track, spacing_km = 10)
as.data.frame(samples)[c("feature_id", "distance_km", "depth", "time",
                         "support_km")]
```

Each point is then buffered and looped over as above. Here each buffer is a
circle of 3 km radius, from 10 m above to 10 m below its point. Its values
come from the time step nearest the point's time, which `as_voxel()` picks
when given the point:

```{r track-loop}
sample_buffers <- buffer_3d(samples, radius_km = 3, depth_window = 10)
local <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(sample_buffers), function(i) {
  b <- sample_buffers[i]
  v <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, b), time = samples[i])[[1]]
  cbind(feature_id = as.data.frame(b)$feature_id,
        summarise_3d(suppressMessages(mask(v, b)), statistic = "mean"))
}))
local
```

Each row is a local summary: the conditions inside one buffer. A track
summary describes the sequence of those local summaries. Weighting each one
by `support_km` gives the mean along the distance travelled, so a stretch of
route sampled more densely doesn't count for more. `support_seconds` weights
by the time spent instead.

```{r track-summary}
stats::weighted.mean(local$mean, as.data.frame(samples)$support_km)
```

This is the mean of the local means along the route, not a mean over all
the water the buffers cover. Neighbouring buffers can overlap and use the
same cells, so the local summaries aren't independent of each other.

`sample_3d()` doesn't yet check that each segment stays in water, and the
package has no "most similar value" summary or interpolated targets along a
track (#105).

## Areas: a protected area down to 50 m

An area is a polygon with a depth range. This one covers the middle of the
grid, from the surface to 50 m:

```{r area}
mpa <- sf::st_sf(
  name = "reef",
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(
    c(150.3, -20.7), c(150.7, -20.7), c(150.7, -20.3), c(150.3, -20.3),
    c(150.3, -20.7)
  ))), crs = 4326)
)
reef <- as_vector3d(mpa, depth_min = 0, depth_max = 50)
volume(reef) # km³
```

The area has no time, so pick the time step with a date. `by = "depth"` gives
one row per depth level:

```{r area-profile}
v <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, reef), time = "2020-03-03")
summarise_3d(mask(v, reef), statistic = c("mean", "min", "max"),
             by = "depth")
```

The 50 m level counts because the water it stands for, from 37.5 m to 75 m,
overlaps the area's depth range; `vignette("depth-levels")` describes this
rule.
The 100 m and 200 m levels are outside the area, so their rows have `NA` and
`n = 0`.

## Through time: habitat volume per day

`volume()` on the proxy measures each time step in turn, in km³. Pass `fun`
to count only some values as habitat, here water between 24 and 26 °C:

```{r volume-time}
volume(proxy, fun = function(x) x >= 24 & x <= 26)
```

The habitat shrinks from day to day because the synthetic water warms each
day.

For the habitat inside the area only, keep the habitat in one day's voxel
with `occupied()`. Masking it by the area would keep whole depth levels, so
the 50 m level would count water down to 75 m, below the area's floor.
Instead, turn the habitat into a depth range per cell with
`voxel_to_envelope()` and intersect it with the area, which cuts it at 50 m:

```{r volume-area}
habitat <- occupied(v, function(x) x >= 24 & x <= 26)
inside <- intersect_3d(voxel_to_envelope(habitat), reef)
volume(inside) # km³
```

## Putting the rows together

The buffer loop ends with a list of data frames, one per buffer, each starting
with the buffer's `feature_id`. `do.call(rbind, ...)` joins them into one
table, which you can then join back to the observations by ID. In the result,
`date` is the detection date and `time` is the time step the values come from:

```{r join}
results <- do.call(rbind, buffer_rows)
merge(obs, results, by.x = "tag", by.y = "feature_id")
```
